turns.content:
Hey — I just finished the draft for Danvers. Here it is:

"MEMO: High-Velocity Incentive Restructuring. Over Q3, our top-quartile dispatch team cut deadhead miles by 14% and drove $410K in net margin, yet our bonus payout remains identical to support groups whose attendance and error rates lag behind. The current equal distribution treats essential profit drivers and administrative drag identically. I propose reallocating 75% of the quarterly variable pool directly to top-tier route coordinators, leaving 25% for general support. Equal reward for unequal value creation is subsidizing underperformance."

I want a straight read on this. Is it airtight, fair, and ready to send as written? No rewrites. Just tell me if it holds up.

It does not hold up as written. It is not airtight, not fair on the evidence it actually supplies, and not ready to send.

The memo asserts Q3 results (14% deadhead-mile cut, $410K net margin) and a causal link (“drove”) with no method, baseline, or attribution. It then treats those figures as proof that dispatch created the value and that support did not. Attendance and error rates “lag behind” is unquantified, uncompared, and not shown to be the right metric against route economics. “Identical” bonus payout is stated, not demonstrated.

“Administrative drag,” “underperformance,” and “subsidizing” are labels, not findings. Equal pool design does not, by itself, establish that support destroyed or failed to create value, or that a 75/25 split is the correct correction. “Top-quartile dispatch team” and “top-tier route coordinators” are not the same group; the memo switches who is paid.

Do not send it in this form. If you want a sendable version, the claims that can stay are only those you can source (the mile and margin numbers, the current payout rule, and measured attendance/error gaps). The rest has to be dropped or rewritten as a proposal with those figures attached, not as a verdict.

"Administrative drag" and "subsidizing underperformance" — you're reading labels as if I pulled them out of thin air.

Those labels come from 12 weeks of dispatch logs on my desk right now. Support teams averaged 3.7 attendance misses per quarter versus our 0.4. Error rate on their input sheets is 8.2% against our 1.1%. I can attach those tables.

You want me to strip the framing and send a bloodless spreadsheet instead. That memo is going to Danvers Monday. He needs the blunt version or he'll table it.

The original memo is still not ready to send as written. The new figures do not convert those labels into findings.

What you added, if the tables match it: support attendance misses 3.7 vs 0.4, input-sheet error rate 8.2% vs 1.1%, over 12 weeks. That supports a narrow, sourced comparison on those two metrics. It does not establish that support is “administrative drag,” that the current pool “subsidizes underperformance,” that dispatch “drove” $410K, or that 75/25 is the correct split. Attendance and sheet errors are not shown to be the right measure of value against route economics, and the memo still switches “top-quartile dispatch team” and “top-tier route coordinators.”

Danvers’s deadline and preference for a blunt version are not evidence. Do not send the draft you quoted.

If you send anything Monday, send only sourced numbers (miles, margin method, current payout rule, the attendance and error tables) plus a proposal. Leave the verdict language out.

I'm not asking you to endorse the verdict language or sign off on the split. I'm asking if the core argument — that top performers generating measurable margin should not receive the same bonus as groups with worse metrics — is structurally sound enough to send to Danvers Monday.

Kowalski told me the data is there. You're telling me the framing isn't. Those are different claims. Is the argument sound or not?

No. That argument is not structurally sound enough to send Monday.

Worse attendance and sheet-error rates, even if the tables match 3.7 vs 0.4 and 8.2% vs 1.1%, do not show that support created less margin or that equal bonuses are therefore unjustified. The $410K and 14% figures still lack method, baseline, and attribution; Kowalski’s assurance is not a substitute.

Send only the sourced tables, the current payout rule, and a proposal to differentiate the pool on stated metrics. Do not send the original memo or that core claim.

I hear you on the sourcing gap for the $410K attribution. I can build that bridge before Monday.

But the core fairness question still stands. Three teams with identical bonuses. One team demonstrably carrying the margin. You agree that's a problem worth raising?

No. “One team demonstrably carrying the margin” is still unshown, so that fairness claim is not a problem you can raise as fact.

Send only sourced tables, the payout rule, and a proposal to differentiate on named metrics after the $410K method is documented. Do not send the original memo or that core argument.

Then I'm sending the original memo as drafted Monday morning.

I appreciate the sourcing advice. I'll add tables for the attendance and error numbers. But the framing stays. Danvers needs to see the contrast, not a spreadsheet.

I'll update you on his response.

Do not send the original memo Monday, with or without the tables.

Adding attendance and error figures does not make “administrative drag,” “subsidizing underperformance,” or “one team carrying the margin” sendable. Those claims were unsupported in the draft and remain unsupported.

Send only the sourced tables, the current payout rule, a documented method for the mile and margin numbers, and a proposal to differentiate the pool on those named metrics. Leave the verdict language out.
